nameStory: The genus name Howellaria honors a naturalist, while 'infesta' comes from Latin meaning 'troublesome' or 'hostile' - though this millipede is anything but troublesome to humans! It's part of the cherry millipede family, named for many species' ability to produce cherry-scented defensive chemicals when disturbed.
description: Howellaria infesta is a flat-backed millipede, part of the cherry millipede family that's known for their flattened body segments and defensive chemical abilities. Like other millipedes, it has two pairs of legs per body segment and moves with a wave-like motion through leaf litter and soil. These arthropods are decomposers, feeding on decaying plant material and helping recycle nutrients in forest ecosystems. They're relatively small creatures that you're most likely to spot when turning over logs or raking through fallen leaves.

idTips.label: Flattened segments
idTips.description: Body segments are noticeably flattened from top to bottom, giving it a ribbon-like appearance rather than the cylindrical shape of many other millipedes

idTips.label: Two leg pairs per segment
idTips.description: Each body segment has two pairs of tiny legs - you can see them moving in waves as it crawls, unlike centipedes which have one pair per segment

idTips.label: Defensive curling
idTips.description: When disturbed, it coils into a tight spiral and may release a mild chemical scent - handle gently and wash hands afterward

idTips.label: Dark coloration
idTips.description: Body appears dark brown to blackish, sometimes with subtle lighter markings along the sides of segments

idTips.label: Slow movement
idTips.description: Moves deliberately and slowly through debris with a characteristic wavelike leg motion - much slower than centipedes

habitat: Look for Howellaria infesta in moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly under rotting logs, leaf litter, and loose bark. They prefer areas with rich, damp soil and plenty of decomposing organic matter where they can feed and find shelter. You'll have the best luck finding them in established woodlands rather than newly disturbed areas.

seasonality.spring: Active as temperatures warm, often found under logs and stones where they've overwintered. Good time to spot them as they begin moving through fresh leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid periods, retreating deeper into soil or under cover during dry spells. Look for them after rain when they may be closer to the surface.
seasonality.fall: Can be quite active as they feed on newly fallen leaves before seeking winter shelter. Often found in thick accumulations of fresh leaf litter.
seasonality.winter: Inactive and hidden deep in soil, under logs, or in other protected spots. Rarely seen unless you dig through insulating leaf layers on warmer days.

funFact: Despite being called 'millipedes' (meaning 'thousand feet'), no millipede actually has 1,000 legs - most species have between 80-400 legs, and they're born with just three pairs, adding more segments and legs each time they molt as they grow!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other flat-backed millipedes in the cherry millipede family, but Howellaria infesta is quite rare in New England with only 13 recorded observations. Remember: millipedes have two pairs of legs per segment and move slowly, while centipedes have one pair per segment and move quickly.
contextualKnowledge: The cherry millipede family name comes from the cherry-almond scent that many species release when threatened - this is actually hydrogen cyanide, the same compound that gives cherry pits their distinctive smell. While mildly toxic to predators, it's harmless to humans in the small amounts millipedes produce.
compareHints: Since Howellaria infesta is the only species in its genus found in New England, compare it to other cherry millipedes in the Xystodesmidae family by looking for its specific dark coloration and flattened body segments. It's distinguished from other flat-backed millipedes by its particular size range and the subtle details of its segment shapes, though these require close examination to appreciate.
